intuition: A word match is a connected path through cells, not a collection of letter counts. A board may contain enough copies of every letter and still have no legal ordering. Conversely, repeated letters in the word require distinct cells, because a path cannot reuse a square.

The recursive state consists of a coordinate and the next word index. A mismatch or out-of-bounds coordinate immediately rejects that branch. On a match, temporarily mark the square unavailable and search the four neighbors for the next character. This marker represents only the current path’s occupancy.

Restoration is as important as marking. A failed path must not prevent a different starting cell or a different branch from using the same board cell. Restore before returning even when a complete word was found, so the caller receives its original board. The terminal index condition means all earlier characters have already matched; it does not require stepping onto an additional square.

Before searching, reject a word longer than the board or needing more copies of any letter than are available. These are necessary conditions, not proof of adjacency: passing them still requires the full path search. An optional refinement can search the reversed word when its final letter is rarer than its first; reversing a legal path preserves adjacency and no-reuse, reducing the number of candidate starts. The reference retains forward traversal for a consistent walkthrough.

steps: For word="ABCCED", start at the A in board row 0, column 0.
Match B at (0,1), then C at (0,2), marking each visited square so this path cannot return to it.
The next C is directly below at (1,2). From there, E at (2,2) extends the matched prefix.
D at (2,1) completes the six letters. The next recursive index equals the word length, establishing success.
Unwind the recursion and restore every marked letter. Return true for the valid A→B→C→C→E→D path.

codeNotes.note: The temporary marker blocks only cells already on the current recursive path, preventing illegal reuse without a separate visited set.
A neighboring coordinate is searched against the next character, preserving adjacency and character order together.
Restoration runs after both successful and failed searches, so sibling paths and future calls see the original board.
